# Setup

```{r}
#| label: load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(cmdstanr)
library(emmeans)
library(reformulas)
library(easystats)
library(modelbased)
library(tidybayes)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
library(here)

options(
  scipen = 999,
  marginaleffects_posterior_center = mean,
  brms.short_summary = TRUE,
  rms.backend = Sys.getenv("BRMS_BACKEND", "cmdstanr"),
  brms.threads = as.numeric(Sys.getenv("BRMS_THREADS", 2)),
  mc.cores = as.numeric(Sys.getenv("MAX_CORES", 4))
)
```

Shared preprocessing lives in `Scripts/data_prep.R`, producing `explicit_ai` and `explicit_di` from a single exclusion pipeline so the two groups can't drift out of sync on criteria.

```{r}
#| label: data
source(here("Scripts", "data_prep.R"))
```

## Model parameterization

Both groups are modeled with a hierarchical Bayesian drift diffusion model (the Wiener process; Ratcliff, 1978), fit via `brms` (Bürkner, 2017) through Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) with the `cmdstanr` backend. Each trial's response time and binary choice are decomposed into **drift rate** (`mu`), **non-decision time** (`ndt`), **starting point** (`bias`), and **boundary separation** (`bs`).

`mu`, `ndt`, `bias`, and `bs` each get the full `condition * dist * age.group` factorial structure, coded as `0 + condition:dist:age.group` — one directly-interpretable parameter per condition x dist x age group cell, rather than a main-effects-plus-interactions decomposition. This coding is necessary for a shared prior scale on every coefficient to translate into an equal implied prior on every cell's mean: a prior-predictive check (posterior draws generated from the prior alone, likelihood switched off) showed that the conventional decomposition gives up to 2.7-fold differences in implied prior SD across cells — systematically tighter for cells reached via fewer summed coefficients — while the cell-means coding used here flattens that to within 5-11%. By-subject random intercepts and slopes for `dist` are included on `mu` in both groups (`(1 + dist | p | sn)`). In the AI group, `bs` and `bias` now share that same random-effects structure too (one correlated 6-dimensional block per subject, rather than three independent 2-dimensional ones) — a re-attempt of something that previously produced severe divergences, back when `bs` and `bias` lacked the full factorial fixed-effects structure they have now; see `ddm-ai.qmd`'s Priors section for the convergence diagnostics and an explicit check of how weakly identified the resulting variance/correlation parameters are. The DI group's `bs`/`bias` random effects have not yet been revisited and remain as they were: `ndt` has no random effects in either group, and DI's `bs`/`bias` don't either — for `ndt`, this is a genuine identifiability limit (too few trials per subject per cell to separate its individual differences from `mu`'s), not merely a missing-fixed-effects-structure issue.

Fixed-effect priors are identical in structure for both groups: `normal(0, 1)` on every `mu` and `bias` coefficient, `normal(0.3, 0.1)` bounded to `[0, min_Y]` on every `ndt` coefficient, `normal(2, 1)` bounded to `[0, Inf)` on every `bs` coefficient (centered near each group's earlier pooled single-parameter estimate, \~2.6-2.7). `bs`'s prior needed to be specified explicitly once it got a `0 + ...` predictor formula — that coding drops `brms`'s default positivity constraint on a parameter-less `bs`, leaving an unbounded flat prior on the coefficients unless one is set, so positivity here is enforced by the prior's lower bound rather than the (identity) link.

The random-effect SD priors now differ between groups, though: both use `normal(0, 0.03)` on `mu`'s by-subject random effects, but only AI additionally has this same `0.03` scale on `bs` and `bias`'s random effects (`dpar = bs`/`dpar = bias`), since only AI's `bs`/`bias` random effects have been revisited and refit so far. `0.03` is a deliberately tight, project-specific choice, not a field-standard default — see `ddm-ai.qmd`'s "Justification for the random-effect prior scale" for the full case (sparse per-subject trial counts, this project's own divergence history, a direct head-to-head test against `HDDM`'s much wider default priors that reproduces the failure mode in a form Stan's divergence diagnostic doesn't catch, and a robustness check showing the substantive results don't depend on this choice).

```{r}
#| label: family
family_wiener <- wiener(link_bs = "identity", link_ndt = "identity", link_bias = "logit")
```

Credibility throughout is defined as the 95% credible interval excluding zero together with `pd > 97.5%`. ROPE percentages are available in the extracted results objects but are not the basis for calling an effect credible.

```{r}
#| label: sampler-settings
n_chains <- 4
n_iter <- 10000
n_warmup <- 500
n_thin <- 10
adapt_delta_val <- .95
max_treedepth_val <- 15
n_postwarmup_draws <- (n_iter - n_warmup) / n_thin * n_chains
```

```{r}
#| label: shared-helpers
normalize_eq_minus_uneq <- function(df) {
  flip <- df$Level1 == "uneq"
  if (any(flip)) {
    new_low <- -df$CI_high[flip]
    new_high <- -df$CI_low[flip]
    df$Difference[flip] <- -df$Difference[flip]
    df$CI_low[flip] <- new_low
    df$CI_high[flip] <- new_high
    tmp <- df$Level1[flip]
    df$Level1[flip] <- df$Level2[flip]
    df$Level2[flip] <- tmp
  }
  df
}

rope_scale <- function(fit, dpar) {
  draws <- posterior_epred(fit, dpar = dpar)
  0.1 * sd(as.vector(draws))
}

filter_row <- function(df, ...) {
  filters <- list(...)
  row <- df
  for (col in names(filters)) row <- row[row[[col]] == filters[[col]], ]
  if (nrow(row) != 1) stop("filter matched ", nrow(row), " rows, expected 1")
  row
}

fmt_contrast <- function(df, ...) {
  row <- filter_row(df, ...)
  sprintf(
    "%s, 95%% CI [%s, %s], *pd* = %s%%",
    insight::format_value(row$Difference),
    insight::format_value(row$CI_low),
    insight::format_value(row$CI_high),
    insight::format_value(row$pd * 100, digits = 1)
  )
}

fmt_mean <- function(df, ...) {
  row <- filter_row(df, ...)
  value_col <- setdiff(names(df), c(names(list(...)), "CI_low", "CI_high", "pd", "ROPE_Percentage"))
  sprintf("%s, 95%% CI [%s, %s]", insight::format_value(row[[value_col]]), insight::format_value(row$CI_low), insight::format_value(row$CI_high))
}

credible_label <- function(df, ..., pd_threshold = 0.975) {
  row <- filter_row(df, ...)
  ci_excludes_zero <- (row$CI_low > 0) || (row$CI_high < 0)
  if (ci_excludes_zero && row$pd > pd_threshold) "credible" else "not credible"
}

count_credible <- function(df, pd_threshold = 0.975) {
  sum((df$CI_low > 0 | df$CI_high < 0) & df$pd > pd_threshold)
}
```

# Advantageous Inequity (AI) Group

```{r}
#| label: ai-formula
formula_ai <- bf(
  duration | dec(dec_recode) ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group +
    (1 + dist | p | sn),
  ndt ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group,
  bias ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group +
    (1 + dist | p | sn),
  bs ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group +
    (1 + dist | p | sn)
)

# bs and bias share mu's group id p, so brms estimates one correlated
# 6-dimensional random-effects block (intercept + dist slope, for each of
# mu/bs/bias) per subject rather than three independent 2-dimensional ones.
# See ddm-ai.qmd's "Are these priors weakly identified?" for why the sd
# priors below are deliberately tight (and how that compares to HDDM's
# much wider defaults), and for the convergence diagnostics this produced.
bprior_ai <-
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = b) +
  prior(normal(0.3, 0.1), class = b, dpar = ndt, lb = 0, ub = "min_Y") +
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = b, dpar = bias) +
  prior(normal(2, 1), class = b, dpar = bs, lb = 0) +
  prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = sd, group = sn, lb = 0) +
  prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = sd, dpar = bs, group = sn, lb = 0) +
  prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = sd, dpar = bias, group = sn, lb = 0)

tmp_dat_ai <- make_standata(formula_ai, family = family_wiener, data = explicit_ai, prior = bprior_ai)

initfun_ai <- function() {
  list(
    b = rnorm(tmp_dat_ai$K, 0, 0.2),
    b_bs = rnorm(tmp_dat_ai$K_bs, 2, 0.3),
    b_ndt = runif(tmp_dat_ai$K_ndt, 0.001, 0.05),
    b_bias = rnorm(tmp_dat_ai$K_bias, 0, 0.1),
    sd_1 = runif(tmp_dat_ai$M_1, 0.05, 0.1),
    z_1 = matrix(rnorm(tmp_dat_ai$M_1 * tmp_dat_ai$N_1, 0, 0.01), tmp_dat_ai$M_1, tmp_dat_ai$N_1),
    L_1 = diag(tmp_dat_ai$M_1)
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: ai-fit
fit_ai <- brm(formula_ai,
  data = explicit_ai,
  family = family_wiener,
  prior = bprior_ai, init = initfun_ai,
  chains = n_chains, cores = n_chains,
  iter = n_iter, warmup = n_warmup, sample_prior = TRUE,
  save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE), thin = n_thin,
  file = here("analysis", "models", "ai_ddm_3way_bs_bias_re"),
  control = list(adapt_delta = adapt_delta_val, max_treedepth = max_treedepth_val),
  backend = "cmdstanr", threads = threading(2)
)

summary(fit_ai)
```

```{r}
#| label: ai-contrasts
rope_mu_ai <- rope_scale(fit_ai, "mu")
rope_ndt_ai <- rope_scale(fit_ai, "ndt")
rope_bias_ai <- rope_scale(fit_ai, "bias")
rope_bs_ai <- rope_scale(fit_ai, "bs")

contrasts_mu_ai <- estimate_contrasts(fit_ai, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "mu", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_mu_ai, rope_mu_ai)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
contrasts_ndt_ai <- estimate_contrasts(fit_ai, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "ndt", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_ndt_ai, rope_ndt_ai)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
contrasts_bias_ai <- estimate_contrasts(fit_ai, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "bias", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_bias_ai, rope_bias_ai)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
bias_by_condition_ai <- estimate_means(fit_ai, by = "condition", predict = "bias", backend = "emmeans")
contrasts_bs_ai <- estimate_contrasts(fit_ai, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "bs", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_bs_ai, rope_bs_ai)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
bs_by_condition_ai <- estimate_means(fit_ai, by = "condition", predict = "bs", backend = "emmeans")

# Simple main effects (age, condition, dist -- each marginal over the other
# two factors), alongside the cell-level dist-by-condition-by-age contrasts
# above. See ddm-ai.qmd's "Main effects" section for the full versions.
main_effect_means_ai <- function(dpar, by) estimate_means(fit_ai, by = by, predict = dpar, backend = "emmeans")
main_effect_contrasts_ai <- function(dpar, contrast) estimate_contrasts(fit_ai, contrast = contrast, predict = dpar, backend = "emmeans")

for (dp in c("mu", "ndt", "bias", "bs")) {
  assign(paste0(dp, "_by_age_ai"), main_effect_means_ai(dp, "age.group"))
  assign(paste0(dp, "_by_cond_ai"), main_effect_means_ai(dp, "condition"))
  assign(paste0(dp, "_by_dist_ai"), main_effect_means_ai(dp, "dist"))
  assign(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_age_ai"), main_effect_contrasts_ai(dp, "age.group"))
  assign(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_cond_ai"), main_effect_contrasts_ai(dp, "condition"))
  assign(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_dist_ai"), main_effect_contrasts_ai(dp, "dist") |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq())
}
```

## Results

**Drift rate.** At 4–5 years — the youngest age tested — autonomous (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "4&5")`, `r credible_label(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "4&5")`) and baseline (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "baseline", age.group = "4&5")`, `r credible_label(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "baseline", age.group = "4&5")`) show little evidence that children differentiate between equal and unequal outcomes, but the norm condition already does (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "norm", age.group = "4&5")`). This pattern persists at 6–7 years: norm remains credible (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "norm", age.group = "6&7")`), while autonomous (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "6&7")`, `r credible_label(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "6&7")`) and baseline (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "baseline", age.group = "6&7")`, `r credible_label(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "baseline", age.group = "6&7")`) remain non-credible. By 8–9 years, credible distinctions are evident in all three conditions: autonomous, `r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "8&9")`; baseline, `r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "baseline", age.group = "8&9")`; and norm, `r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_ai, condition = "norm", age.group = "8&9")`. The emergence of credible effects in the autonomous and baseline conditions at 8–9 years aligns with developmental work suggesting that advantageous inequity aversion typically emerges around this age (Blake & McAuliffe, 2011). Norm's credibility from the youngest age tested onward suggests that explicit fairness framing does not just pull that sensitivity forward to an intermediate age, but makes it detectable years earlier than it otherwise appears.

**Non-decision time.** In contrast to drift rate, non-decision time shows little evidence of a systematic equal-vs.-unequal distinction. Credible effects emerge in only `r count_credible(contrasts_ndt_ai)` of the 9 condition-by-age cells, and these effects differ in direction and do not form a consistent developmental or condition-specific pattern. Thus, there is little indication that the fairness manipulation operates through changes in non-decision processes.

**Starting point.** Starting-point estimates are also highly similar across conditions (autonomous = `r fmt_mean(bias_by_condition_ai, condition = "autonomous")`; baseline = `r fmt_mean(bias_by_condition_ai, condition = "baseline")`; norm = `r fmt_mean(bias_by_condition_ai, condition = "norm")`), with no credible differences between conditions. Equal-vs.-unequal contrasts in starting-point bias are likewise largely absent, with only `r count_credible(contrasts_bias_ai)` of the 9 condition-by-age cells reaching credibility and no clear developmental or condition-specific pattern.

**Boundary separation.** Unlike starting point, boundary separation shows a clear secondary pattern that tracks condition, and closely tracks drift rate's own timeline rather than leading or lagging it. Equal-vs.-unequal contrasts are credible in `r count_credible(contrasts_bs_ai)` of the 9 condition-by-age cells, uniformly in the direction of wider boundaries on equal-split trials. This pattern is most pronounced in the norm condition, where the contrast is already credible at 4–5 years (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bs_ai, condition = "norm", age.group = "4&5")`) — the same age at which drift rate's norm contrast first becomes credible — and remains credible through 8–9 years (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bs_ai, condition = "norm", age.group = "8&9")`). The autonomous condition reaches credibility only at 8–9 years (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bs_ai, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "8&9")`), matching drift rate's own autonomous timeline, and the baseline condition does not reach credibility at any age tested, even though drift rate's baseline contrast does become credible at 8–9 years — boundary separation's credible cells are essentially a subset of drift rate's, not an independent or earlier-arriving signal. Consistent with this pattern, norm also shows the widest marginal boundary separation of the three conditions (autonomous = `r fmt_mean(bs_by_condition_ai, condition = "autonomous")`; baseline = `r fmt_mean(bs_by_condition_ai, condition = "baseline")`; norm = `r fmt_mean(bs_by_condition_ai, condition = "norm")`). This pattern should be read with more caution than drift rate's: a formal prior-sensitivity check (`ddm-ai.qmd`, Priors > Prior sensitivity check) found that 3 of these 4 credible cells lose credibility under a weakly informative random-effect prior, leaving only norm@8-9y, while drift rate's own findings are comparatively stable under the same check.

Taken together, the effect of the fairness prompt on advantageous inequity aversion is concentrated primarily in drift rate, with boundary separation serving as a secondary, norm-specific locus present on essentially the same timeline as drift rate itself rather than emerging ahead of it — though, unlike drift rate, this secondary role depends substantially on the random-effect prior's scale (`ddm-ai.qmd`, Priors > Prior sensitivity check). Starting-point bias and non-decision time show little evidence of systematic involvement. The prompt therefore appears to influence how strongly and how early children accumulate evidence differently for equal versus unequal outcomes, and — specifically under explicit fairness framing, and with the above caveat — how much evidence they require before committing to a response, rather than altering their initial response bias or the time required for perceptual and motor processes.

# Disadvantageous Inequity (DI) Group

```{r}
#| label: di-formula
formula_di <- bf(
  duration | dec(dec_recode) ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group +
    (1 + dist | p | sn),
  ndt ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group,
  bias ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group +
    (1 + dist | p | sn),
  bs ~ 0 + condition:dist:age.group +
    (1 + dist | p | sn)
)

# bs and bias share mu's group id p here too, matching the AI section above --
# see ddm-di.qmd and ddm-ai.qmd's Priors sections for the full justification
# and convergence diagnostics.
bprior_di <-
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = b) +
  prior(normal(0.3, 0.1), class = b, dpar = ndt, lb = 0, ub = "min_Y") +
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = b, dpar = bias) +
  prior(normal(2, 1), class = b, dpar = bs, lb = 0) +
  prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = sd, group = sn, lb = 0) +
  prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = sd, dpar = bs, group = sn, lb = 0) +
  prior(normal(0, 0.03), class = sd, dpar = bias, group = sn, lb = 0)

tmp_dat_di <- make_standata(formula_di, family = family_wiener, data = explicit_di, prior = bprior_di)

initfun_di <- function() {
  list(
    b = rnorm(tmp_dat_di$K, 0, 0.2),
    b_bs = rnorm(tmp_dat_di$K_bs, 2, 0.3),
    b_ndt = runif(tmp_dat_di$K_ndt, 0.001, 0.05),
    b_bias = rnorm(tmp_dat_di$K_bias, 0, 0.1),
    sd_1 = runif(tmp_dat_di$M_1, 0.05, 0.1),
    z_1 = matrix(rnorm(tmp_dat_di$M_1 * tmp_dat_di$N_1, 0, 0.01), tmp_dat_di$M_1, tmp_dat_di$N_1),
    L_1 = diag(tmp_dat_di$M_1)
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: di-fit
fit_di <- brm(formula_di,
  data = explicit_di,
  family = family_wiener,
  prior = bprior_di, init = initfun_di,
  chains = n_chains, cores = n_chains,
  iter = n_iter, warmup = n_warmup, sample_prior = TRUE,
  save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE), thin = n_thin,
  file = here("analysis", "models", "di_3way_bs_bias_re"),
  control = list(adapt_delta = adapt_delta_val, max_treedepth = max_treedepth_val),
  backend = "cmdstanr", threads = threading(2)
)

summary(fit_di)
```

```{r}
#| label: di-contrasts
rope_mu_di <- rope_scale(fit_di, "mu")
rope_ndt_di <- rope_scale(fit_di, "ndt")
rope_bias_di <- rope_scale(fit_di, "bias")
rope_bs_di <- rope_scale(fit_di, "bs")

contrasts_mu_di <- estimate_contrasts(fit_di, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "mu", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_mu_di, rope_mu_di)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
contrasts_ndt_di <- estimate_contrasts(fit_di, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "ndt", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_ndt_di, rope_ndt_di)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
contrasts_bias_di <- estimate_contrasts(fit_di, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "bias", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_bias_di, rope_bias_di)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
bias_by_condition_di <- estimate_means(fit_di, by = "condition", predict = "bias", backend = "emmeans")
contrasts_bs_di <- estimate_contrasts(fit_di, contrast = "dist", by = c("condition", "age.group"),
  predict = "bs", backend = "emmeans", rope_range = c(-rope_bs_di, rope_bs_di)) |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq()
bs_by_condition_di <- estimate_means(fit_di, by = "condition", predict = "bs", backend = "emmeans")

# Simple main effects (age, condition, dist), same as the ai-contrasts chunk above.
main_effect_means_di <- function(dpar, by) estimate_means(fit_di, by = by, predict = dpar, backend = "emmeans")
main_effect_contrasts_di <- function(dpar, contrast) estimate_contrasts(fit_di, contrast = contrast, predict = dpar, backend = "emmeans")

for (dp in c("mu", "ndt", "bias", "bs")) {
  assign(paste0(dp, "_by_age_di"), main_effect_means_di(dp, "age.group"))
  assign(paste0(dp, "_by_cond_di"), main_effect_means_di(dp, "condition"))
  assign(paste0(dp, "_by_dist_di"), main_effect_means_di(dp, "dist"))
  assign(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_age_di"), main_effect_contrasts_di(dp, "age.group"))
  assign(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_cond_di"), main_effect_contrasts_di(dp, "condition"))
  assign(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_dist_di"), main_effect_contrasts_di(dp, "dist") |> normalize_eq_minus_uneq())
}
```

## Results

**Drift rate.** In contrast to advantageous inequity, children distinguish between equal and disadvantageously unequal outcomes from the youngest age tested, and this distinction is evident regardless of prompt condition. At 4–5 years, credible equal-vs.-unequal differences are already present in the autonomous (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_di, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "4&5")`), baseline (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_di, condition = "baseline", age.group = "4&5")`), and norm conditions (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_di, condition = "norm", age.group = "4&5")`). This pattern generalizes to the other age groups. Thus, unlike advantageous inequity, explicit fairness framing does not appear necessary for the distinction to emerge. Indeed, at 6–7 years the norm condition shows the smallest effect (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_di, condition = "norm", age.group = "6&7")`), relative to baseline (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_di, condition = "baseline", age.group = "6&7")`) and autonomous (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_mu_di, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "6&7")`). This pattern contrasts with advantageous inequity, where the norm condition showed the earliest and strongest differentiation.

**Non-decision time.** In contrast to drift rate, non-decision time shows no evidence of a systematic equal-vs.-unequal distinction. Credible effects emerge in `r count_credible(contrasts_ndt_di)` of the 9 condition-by-age cells, indicating that the disadvantageous-inequity effect is unlikely to reflect differences in perceptual, encoding, or motor processes. This mirrors the pattern observed for advantageous inequity.

**Starting point.** Starting-point bias showed a more limited developmental effect. Equal-vs.-unequal differences became credible at 6–7 years in the autonomous (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bias_di, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "6&7")`) and baseline conditions (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bias_di, condition = "baseline", age.group = "6&7")`) and remained credible at 8–9 years (autonomous: `r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bias_di, condition = "autonomous", age.group = "8&9")`; baseline: `r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bias_di, condition = "baseline", age.group = "8&9")`). No corresponding effect emerged in the norm condition at any age. Despite these within-condition contrasts, overall starting-point estimates were similar across conditions (autonomous = `r fmt_mean(bias_by_condition_di, condition = "autonomous")`; baseline = `r fmt_mean(bias_by_condition_di, condition = "baseline")`; norm = `r fmt_mean(bias_by_condition_di, condition = "norm")`), indicating that the effect was specific to the equal-versus-unequal distinction rather than a general shift in response bias.

**Boundary separation.** Unlike advantageous inequity, boundary separation shows no reliable pattern in this group. Equal-vs.-unequal contrasts are credible in only `r count_credible(contrasts_bs_di)` of the 9 condition-by-age cells, with no shared age or condition trend linking them. Marginal boundary separation also does not differ credibly across conditions (autonomous = `r fmt_mean(bs_by_condition_di, condition = "autonomous")`; baseline = `r fmt_mean(bs_by_condition_di, condition = "baseline")`; norm = `r fmt_mean(bs_by_condition_di, condition = "norm")`). Pooling across condition and age nonetheless recovers a credible marginal equal-vs.-unequal effect (`r fmt_contrast(contrasts_bs_dist_di)`), suggesting a real but diffuse signal rather than the coherent, condition-specific pattern observed for advantageous inequity.

Taken together, disadvantageous inequity aversion is present from the youngest age tested and is largely independent of experimental framing, with the effect concentrated in drift rate. Starting-point bias shows a secondary role specific to the autonomous and baseline conditions, emerging from 6–7 years onward and absent when children were explicitly prompted to be fair — the opposite pattern from advantageous inequity, where boundary separation, not starting point, carried the secondary effect, and specifically in the norm condition. Non-decision time shows no evidence of involvement in either form of inequity aversion.

# Main Effects Summary

Every age, condition, and dist main-effect comparison computed above (all four parameters, both groups), consolidated into one APA-style table rather than scattered across the bullets. A second table below does the same for the cell-level `dist` x `condition` x `age.group` interaction contrasts (the primary results throughout this document). Both are built programmatically from the `contrasts_*` objects already computed above, so neither can drift out of sync with the prose.

**Format.** Both tables follow APA table conventions: a numbered, italicized title above the table; horizontal rules only (above the header, below the header, at the bottom) with no vertical rules; the `Parameter` column grouped with `rowspan` instead of repeating on every row; group and condition/age labels spelled out and title-cased; and a `Note.` line below explaining abbreviations. AI and DI each get a spanning three-column header (`Estimate [95% CrI]`, `pd`, `% in ROPE`) rather than six flat columns repeating "AI"/"DI" in every header.

**Color coding.** `mu` and `bias` estimate cells are shaded by direction, since both share the same sign convention given how `dec_recode` is coded (`dec_recode = 1` = reject boundary): a **red** cell means the comparison shifts evidence/starting-point toward *reject*, a **green** cell means it shifts toward *accept*. Saturation carries credibility — vivid color means the comparison clears the 95% CrI/*pd* bar, pale color means it doesn't. `bs` and `ndt` are deliberately left uncolored: neither points toward either response boundary, so an accept/reject color scheme would misrepresent what they measure. Alternating row shading (light gray) is layered underneath for readability and doesn't override the direction color where one applies.

Both tables are hand-built HTML (`<table>`/`<td>`, not `knitr::kable()`), with every style — background color, borders, alignment — set directly on the `<td>`/`<th>` itself. That combination is what survives copy-pasting the rendered table into Word: Word's HTML importer reliably keeps styling set directly on a table cell, is inconsistent about styling nested inside a cell (e.g. a `<span>`), and `kable()`'s output format isn't guaranteed to be a real `<table>` outside an actual render pipeline.

```{r}
#| label: apa-table-helpers
fmt_est <- function(x) insight::format_value(x, digits = 2)
fmt_ci <- function(lo, hi) sprintf("[%s, %s]", insight::format_value(lo, digits = 2), insight::format_value(hi, digits = 2))
fmt_pd_pct <- function(pd) sprintf("%s%%", insight::format_value(pd * 100, digits = 1))
fmt_rope_pct <- function(rope) sprintf("%s%%", insight::format_value(rope * 100, digits = 1))
is_credible <- function(lo, hi, pd) (lo > 0 | hi < 0) & pd > 0.975

combine_estimate_ci <- function(est, lo, hi) sprintf("%s %s", fmt_est(est), fmt_ci(lo, hi))
combine_pd_credible <- function(pd, lo, hi) {
  pct <- fmt_pd_pct(pd)
  ifelse(is_credible(lo, hi, pd), paste0(pct, " ✓"), pct)
}

# Background color for mu/bias estimate cells only (see prose above for why
# bs/ndt are excluded). Vivid = credible, pale = not; red = reject-ward
# (positive), green = accept-ward (negative). NA = no direction shading
# (the alternating row stripe shows through instead).
cell_bg <- function(difference, lo, hi, pd, dpar) {
  if (!(dpar %in% c("mu", "bias"))) return(NA_character_)
  credible <- is_credible(lo, hi, pd)
  if (difference > 0) {
    if (credible) "#f5b7b1" else "#fdedec"
  } else {
    if (credible) "#a9dfbf" else "#eafaf1"
  }
}

esc_html <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("&", "&amp;", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("<", "&lt;", x, fixed = TRUE)
  gsub(">", "&gt;", x, fixed = TRUE)
}

# Display-label helpers -- code identifiers (mu/ndt/bias/bs, "4&5", "eq") get
# spelled out and title-cased for the table without touching the underlying data.
param_labels <- c(mu = "Drift Rate", ndt = "Non-Decision Time", bias = "Starting Point", bs = "Boundary Separation")
fmt_age_label <- function(x) gsub("&", "–", as.character(x), fixed = TRUE)
fmt_cond_label <- function(x) tools::toTitleCase(as.character(x))
fmt_dist_label <- function(x) ifelse(x == "eq", "Equal", "Unequal")

STRIPE_BG <- "#f6f6f6"
RULE <- "1px solid #000000"
GROUP_RULE <- "1px solid #bbbbbb"

# One <td>. A direction color (bg) takes priority over the alternating row
# stripe; top_rule is a full-width black table rule, group_rule a lighter
# separator between parameter blocks.
apa_td <- function(text, align = "center", bg = NA, stripe = FALSE, rowspan = 1, top_rule = FALSE, group_rule = FALSE) {
  style <- sprintf("padding:5px 12px;text-align:%s;", align)
  if (!is.na(bg)) {
    style <- paste0(style, sprintf("background-color:%s;", bg))
  } else if (stripe) {
    style <- paste0(style, sprintf("background-color:%s;", STRIPE_BG))
  }
  if (top_rule) style <- paste0(style, sprintf("border-top:%s;", RULE))
  else if (group_rule) style <- paste0(style, sprintf("border-top:%s;", GROUP_RULE))
  rs <- if (rowspan > 1) sprintf(' rowspan="%d"', rowspan) else ""
  sprintf('<td style="%s"%s>%s</td>', style, rs, esc_html(text))
}

apa_th <- function(text, align = "center", colspan = 1, rowspan = 1, top_rule = FALSE, bottom_rule = FALSE) {
  style <- sprintf("padding:6px 12px;text-align:%s;font-weight:bold;background-color:#eeeeee;", align)
  if (top_rule) style <- paste0(style, sprintf("border-top:%s;", RULE))
  if (bottom_rule) style <- paste0(style, sprintf("border-bottom:%s;", RULE))
  extra <- ""
  if (colspan > 1) extra <- paste0(extra, sprintf(' colspan="%d"', colspan))
  if (rowspan > 1) extra <- paste0(extra, sprintf(' rowspan="%d"', rowspan))
  sprintf('<th style="%s"%s>%s</th>', style, extra, esc_html(text))
}

# lead_headers: the non-grouped leading column headers (rowspan across both
# header rows); group AI/DI each get a 2-column spanning header underneath.
apa_table_head <- function(lead_headers) {
  top <- paste0(
    paste0(vapply(lead_headers, function(h) apa_th(h, align = "left", rowspan = 2, top_rule = TRUE), character(1)), collapse = ""),
    apa_th("AI", colspan = 3, top_rule = TRUE),
    apa_th("DI", colspan = 3, top_rule = TRUE)
  )
  bottom <- paste0(
    apa_th("Estimate [95% CrI]", bottom_rule = TRUE), apa_th("pd", bottom_rule = TRUE), apa_th("% in ROPE", bottom_rule = TRUE),
    apa_th("Estimate [95% CrI]", bottom_rule = TRUE), apa_th("pd", bottom_rule = TRUE), apa_th("% in ROPE", bottom_rule = TRUE)
  )
  paste0("<thead>\n<tr>", top, "</tr>\n<tr>", bottom, "</tr>\n</thead>\n")
}

# One data row's 6 numeric cells (AI Estimate, AI pd, AI ROPE%, DI Estimate,
# DI pd, DI ROPE%); the caller prepends whatever leading label cells that row needs.
apa_numeric_cells <- function(r, dp, stripe, group_rule) {
  paste0(
    apa_td(combine_estimate_ci(r$Difference_ai, r$CI_low_ai, r$CI_high_ai), bg = cell_bg(r$Difference_ai, r$CI_low_ai, r$CI_high_ai, r$pd_ai, dp), stripe = stripe, group_rule = group_rule),
    apa_td(combine_pd_credible(r$pd_ai, r$CI_low_ai, r$CI_high_ai), stripe = stripe, group_rule = group_rule),
    apa_td(fmt_rope_pct(r$ROPE_Percentage_ai), stripe = stripe, group_rule = group_rule),
    apa_td(combine_estimate_ci(r$Difference_di, r$CI_low_di, r$CI_high_di), bg = cell_bg(r$Difference_di, r$CI_low_di, r$CI_high_di, r$pd_di, dp), stripe = stripe, group_rule = group_rule),
    apa_td(combine_pd_credible(r$pd_di, r$CI_low_di, r$CI_high_di), stripe = stripe, group_rule = group_rule),
    apa_td(fmt_rope_pct(r$ROPE_Percentage_di), stripe = stripe, group_rule = group_rule)
  )
}

apa_table <- function(number, title, lead_headers, body_html, note) {
  paste0(
    sprintf("<p><strong>Table %d</strong></p>\n<p><em>%s</em></p>\n", number, esc_html(title)),
    '<table style="border-collapse:collapse;font-family:\'Times New Roman\',Times,serif;font-size:0.95em;">\n',
    apa_table_head(lead_headers),
    "<tbody>\n", body_html, "\n</tbody>\n</table>\n",
    sprintf('<p style="font-size:0.85em;max-width:700px;"><em>Note.</em> CrI = credible interval; pd = probability of direction; %% in ROPE = percentage of the posterior distribution falling inside a region of practical equivalence to zero (each parameter\'s own scaled range; see Credibility Criterion), reported for supplementary context and not the basis for calling a comparison credible. A check mark (✓) indicates a comparison for which the 95%% credible interval excludes zero and pd &gt; 97.5%%. %s</p>\n', note)
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: main-effects-summary-table
#| results: asis
# factor label -> object-name fragment used by the assign() loops above
# (age.group/dist keep their own name; "condition" was abbreviated to "cond")
factor_suffix <- c(age.group = "age", condition = "cond", dist = "dist")
factor_display <- c(age.group = "Age", condition = "Condition", dist = "Dist")

main_effects_body <- character(0)
row_idx <- 0
for (dp_i in seq_along(c("mu", "ndt", "bias", "bs"))) {
  dp <- c("mu", "ndt", "bias", "bs")[dp_i]
  group_rows <- list()
  for (fac in names(factor_suffix)) {
    suf <- factor_suffix[[fac]]
    ai_df <- get(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_", suf, "_ai"))
    di_df <- get(paste0("contrasts_", dp, "_", suf, "_di"))
    merged <- merge(ai_df, di_df, by = c("Level1", "Level2"), suffixes = c("_ai", "_di"))
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(merged))) {
      r <- merged[i, ]
      lab <- switch(fac,
        age.group = c(fmt_age_label(r$Level1), fmt_age_label(r$Level2)),
        condition = c(fmt_cond_label(r$Level1), fmt_cond_label(r$Level2)),
        dist = c(fmt_dist_label(r$Level1), fmt_dist_label(r$Level2))
      )
      group_rows[[length(group_rows) + 1]] <- list(r = r, factor = factor_display[[fac]], comparison = sprintf("%s vs. %s", lab[1], lab[2]))
    }
  }
  n <- length(group_rows)
  for (j in seq_len(n)) {
    row_idx <- row_idx + 1
    stripe <- (row_idx %% 2 == 0)
    gr <- (j == 1) && (dp_i > 1)
    lead <- if (j == 1) apa_td(param_labels[[dp]], align = "left", rowspan = n, stripe = FALSE, top_rule = FALSE, group_rule = gr) else ""
    row <- paste0(
      lead,
      apa_td(group_rows[[j]]$factor, align = "left", stripe = stripe, group_rule = gr),
      apa_td(group_rows[[j]]$comparison, align = "left", stripe = stripe, group_rule = gr),
      apa_numeric_cells(group_rows[[j]]$r, dp, stripe, gr)
    )
    main_effects_body <- c(main_effects_body, paste0("<tr>", row, "</tr>"))
  }
}

cat(apa_table(
  number = 1,
  title = "Main Effects of Age, Condition, and Split Type on Drift Diffusion Model Parameters (AI and DI Groups)",
  lead_headers = c("Parameter", "Factor", "Comparison"),
  body_html = paste(main_effects_body, collapse = "\n"),
  note = "Comparisons are marginal (averaged over the two factors not shown in that row). mu and Starting Point (bias) estimate cells are shaded by direction (red = reject-ward, green = accept-ward; vivid = credible, pale = not); Boundary Separation and Non-Decision Time are not directionally shaded because neither points toward either response boundary."
))
```

## Interaction (dist x condition x age.group)

```{r}
#| label: interaction-summary-table
#| results: asis
interaction_dfs <- list(
  mu = list(ai = contrasts_mu_ai, di = contrasts_mu_di),
  ndt = list(ai = contrasts_ndt_ai, di = contrasts_ndt_di),
  bias = list(ai = contrasts_bias_ai, di = contrasts_bias_di),
  bs = list(ai = contrasts_bs_ai, di = contrasts_bs_di)
)

interaction_body <- character(0)
row_idx <- 0
for (dp_i in seq_along(c("mu", "ndt", "bias", "bs"))) {
  dp <- c("mu", "ndt", "bias", "bs")[dp_i]
  ai_df <- interaction_dfs[[dp]]$ai
  di_df <- interaction_dfs[[dp]]$di
  merged <- merge(ai_df, di_df, by = c("condition", "age.group"), suffixes = c("_ai", "_di"))
  merged <- merged[order(merged$condition, merged$age.group), ]
  n <- nrow(merged)
  for (j in seq_len(n)) {
    row_idx <- row_idx + 1
    stripe <- (row_idx %% 2 == 0)
    gr <- (j == 1) && (dp_i > 1)
    r <- merged[j, ]
    lead <- if (j == 1) apa_td(param_labels[[dp]], align = "left", rowspan = n, stripe = FALSE, top_rule = FALSE, group_rule = gr) else ""
    row <- paste0(
      lead,
      apa_td(fmt_cond_label(r$condition), align = "left", stripe = stripe, group_rule = gr),
      apa_td(fmt_age_label(r$age.group), align = "left", stripe = stripe, group_rule = gr),
      apa_numeric_cells(r, dp, stripe, gr)
    )
    interaction_body <- c(interaction_body, paste0("<tr>", row, "</tr>"))
  }
}

cat(apa_table(
  number = 2,
  title = "Equal- vs. Unequal-Split Contrasts by Condition and Age (AI and DI Groups)",
  lead_headers = c("Parameter", "Condition", "Age"),
  body_html = paste(interaction_body, collapse = "\n"),
  note = "Estimates are the equal-minus-unequal contrast within each condition x age cell (the primary results throughout this document). mu and Starting Point (bias) estimate cells are shaded by direction (red = reject-ward, green = accept-ward; vivid = credible, pale = not); Boundary Separation and Non-Decision Time are not directionally shaded because neither points toward either response boundary."
))
```

# Combined Figures

Each parameter gets one figure spanning both groups, rows for AI vs. DI and columns for age group, so the two groups' patterns sit directly above and below each other rather than in separate documents. Condition is encoded by both fill color and y-axis position (redundant on purpose, since the labels alone already disambiguate condition — color reinforces rather than carries the identity), using three colors chosen to stay visually distinct for readers with color vision deficiencies as well as typical color vision.

```{r}
  gather_emmeans_draws() |> mutate(group = "AI")
```

# Cross-Group Comparison

Considered together, the two groups indicate that the timing of inequity aversion depends on whose interest is at stake.

Disadvantageous inequity aversion required no prompting. From the youngest age tested (4–5y) through 8–9y, and regardless of whether children were prompted to be fair, told to act autonomously, or given no framing at all, disadvantageous offers were met with credible rejection in every condition. This distinction appears to be present from early childhood and is largely unaffected by experimental framing.

Advantageous inequity aversion followed a slower and more context-dependent trajectory. Left to their own devices (the autonomous and baseline conditions), children did not reliably object to advantageous unfairness until 8–9 years — three to four years later than their objection to disadvantageous unfairness, and consistent with prior developmental work placing advantageous inequity aversion's spontaneous emergence around that age. An explicit fairness prompt, however, brought this sensitivity forward to 4–5 years, the youngest age tested. Advantageous inequity aversion therefore appears to be present but dormant in younger children, requiring either additional development or explicit framing to become detectable.

This asymmetry is located specifically in drift rate rather than in non-decision time, which carried no reliable signal in either group. Each group additionally recruited one secondary parameter, and the two did not overlap. In the disadvantageous group, starting point shifted credibly in the autonomous and baseline conditions from 6–7 years onward, with no corresponding effect in the advantageous group. In the advantageous group, boundary separation showed a credible secondary pattern in the norm condition — wider boundaries on equal-split trials, present on essentially the same timeline as drift rate itself rather than preceding it, with the autonomous condition showing a smaller version of the same pattern by 8–9 years. Boundary separation's credible cells were close to a subset of drift rate's, indicating that this reflects caution and evidence accumulation moving together once fairness was made explicit, rather than an independent or earlier-emerging process. Boundary separation showed no corresponding signal in the disadvantageous group. This asymmetry itself is well supported, but the advantageous group's boundary-separation finding specifically is more prior-sensitive than its drift-rate finding: a formal check substituting a weakly informative random-effect prior (`ddm-ai.qmd`, Priors > Prior sensitivity check) left only one of its four credible cells standing, whereas the disadvantageous group's already-sparse boundary-separation cells were essentially unaffected by the same check. The two forms of inequity aversion are thus asymmetric not only in when they emerge, but in which secondary process — starting point or boundary separation — accompanies drift rate in carrying the effect, with that second half of the asymmetry resting on a less robust footing for the advantageous group.
